hlido_opinion.headline: A narrow, numerate vector index that states its claims as ratios against a named baseline — the rare library whose marketing page reads like a benchmark table.
hlido_opinion.body: turbovec is an in-process vector index for Python and Rust that stores vectors at 2 or 4 bits per dimension using Google Research's TurboQuant and searches the compressed form directly with SIMD kernels. What distinguishes it on the public surface is not the idea — quantised ANN search is a crowded field — but the discipline of the claims. Every headline number is a ratio against a named competitor at a stated bit width (4.4x FAISS FastScan at 4-bit, 2.2x at 2-bit, 7.8x smaller than float32 at 4-bit, 15.5x at 2-bit, 'at matching recall'), and the page carries a 'How it compares' and a 'When to use something else' section — the second of which almost nothing in this category ships. The operational story is equally specific: no training step because the codebook is derived mathematically rather than fitted to your data, so a vector is searchable the moment it is added; sync(path) writes only the delta with one fsync and is described as crash-safe at any byte; filtering takes an id allowlist or bitmask and the kernel skips excluded vectors rather than post-filtering results. It is explicitly a library and not a service — nothing leaves the process — which is the right posture for the local-RAG use case it targets. The gaps are the ones a library of this age would be expected to have: the benchmark figures are the author's own and we did not reproduce them, the published surface is a PyPI project page rather than an independent docs site, and there is no pricing or access question to answer because it is pip-installable open source. For an engineer who already knows they want in-process ANN and is choosing between FAISS and something smaller, this is a serious candidate. For anyone who needs a managed vector database with replication and an API, it is the wrong shape of thing entirely, and the page says so.

tier_rationale: STEADY (85) because the public surface is unusually complete for a young library: an installable artifact, working code samples, explicit input contracts (2-D float32 only, other dtypes raise rather than silently convert), stated durability semantics, and comparative claims pinned to a named baseline and a bit width. It stops short of VITAL because every performance number is self-reported with no third-party reproduction we could verify, and because the project has one public surface (a package page) rather than the documentation, changelog and issue history that would let a buyer judge maintenance.
what_it_does_well: Performance claims are stated as ratios against a named baseline (FAISS FastScan) at a specified bit width, not as bare adjectives
Ships a 'When to use something else' section — an honest scope boundary most libraries in this category omit
No training step: the codebook is derived mathematically, so an added vector is immediately searchable and a removal is described as microseconds
Incremental, crash-safe persistence is specified concretely (sync writes only the delta, one fsync, safe at any byte)
Explicitly in-process and local — the data-residency story needs no further explanation
Input contract is strict and documented: 2-D float32 arrays, other dtypes raise instead of silently converting
what_it_fails_at: Every benchmark figure is self-reported; no independent reproduction is linked and we did not run them
The reviewed public surface is a package registry page, not a project site with docs, changelog and maintenance history
No call-to-action beyond a pip install line — a buyer evaluating seriously has nowhere to go for support terms or a roadmap
'At matching recall' is asserted rather than shown with a recall/latency curve on the public surface
Dual Python/Rust positioning means neither audience gets a dedicated getting-started path
best_for: Teams running retrieval in-process who are memory-bound rather than throughput-bound
Local or offline RAG stacks where nothing may leave the machine
Workloads with continuous inserts and deletes, where a rebuild-to-index step is the actual bottleneck
Rust services that want an embedded index without a sidecar process
not_recommended_for: Anyone who needs a managed, replicated vector service with an HTTP API and an SLA
Buyers who require third-party-verified benchmarks before adopting a performance-critical dependency
Teams that need hybrid lexical-plus-vector search or server-side multi-tenancy
Projects that cannot take on a young single-maintainer dependency in the hot path
red_flags: All comparative performance claims originate from the vendor and are not independently reproduced on any surface we could reach. Treat the 4.4x and 15.5x figures as claims to verify against your own data, not as measured facts.

compared_to.verdict_diff: Qdrant is a vector database — a service with an API, persistence, filtering and clustering. turbovec is a library inside your process. Choose Qdrant when retrieval is shared infrastructure; choose turbovec when it belongs to one application and memory is the constraint.
Pinecone is fully managed and priced per use; turbovec is pip-installable and runs where your code runs. Pinecone wins on operational burden, turbovec on cost and data residency.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Python and Rust library APIs (TurboQuantIndex: add, search, sync, load). An agent building a retrieval layer imports it directly; there is no network surface, so an agent cannot query it remotely without wrapping it in a service of its own.

evidence_urls.claim: 2-4 bit quantisation with SIMD search, in-process for Python and Rust
Comparative claims stated against FAISS FastScan at named bit widths
Incremental crash-safe sync and immediate searchability without a training step
